blocks.text: Picture two data scientists handed the exact same raw dataset and the exact same algorithm. One of them trains a model straight on the raw columns and gets mediocre results. The other spends an afternoon deriving a handful of new columns from those same raw columns, a profit margin here, a price per square foot there, an age bracket somewhere else, before touching the algorithm at all. Their model beats the first one by a wide margin. Same data, same algorithm, wildly different outcome. That gap is feature creation, and it is one of the highest leverage skills in the entire machine learning workflow.
1. Introduction
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417253-822320771.png

A feature, in plain terms, is just one individual measurable input column that your model actually sees when it makes a prediction. Age is a feature. Zip code is a feature. Revenue is a feature. If a column sits in your training dataframe and a model reads a value out of it for every row, that column is a feature, full stop. It sounds almost too simple to bother naming, but naming it clearly matters, because most of what separates an average model from a genuinely good one is not the algorithm at all, it is which features that algorithm gets to look at.

items: A customer's age in a churn prediction dataset
The square footage of a house in a pricing model
The number of words in a product review in a sentiment classifier
A zip code in a fraud detection system

blocks.text: Feature creation is the practice of deriving brand new columns like these from the raw data you already have, rather than just feeding a model whatever arrived in the original file untouched. It is frequently called the highest leverage activity in an entire ML project, and that claim is not exaggeration. Swapping one decent algorithm for another decent algorithm might buy you a percent or two of accuracy. Handing that same algorithm one genuinely well constructed feature can move the needle far more than that, because you are giving the model information it previously had no way to see at all.

blocks.title: Feature creation happens before the model, not inside it
blocks.content: Every technique in this lesson runs entirely in pandas, on your dataframe, before anything touches scikit-learn or any other modeling library. The model never knows or cares that price_per_sqft was derived instead of collected directly. All it sees is a column with a value in it.

blocks.text: This lesson walks through the concrete building blocks of feature creation: arithmetic combinations of existing columns, binning a continuous column into discrete buckets, and interaction features that capture what two columns mean together. It closes with a worked example on a real estate dataset that puts all three to work on the same dataframe at once.
2. Arithmetic Combinations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417255-833935090.png

The simplest category of feature creation is also one of the most powerful: taking two or more existing numeric columns and combining them with basic arithmetic, addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, to produce a brand new column that was not literally present in the raw data but is completely derivable from it.

What makes this category so effective is that the resulting number is often far more directly predictive of whatever you are trying to model than either raw input column was on its own. Revenue alone tells a model very little about whether a business is healthy. Cost alone tells it even less. Divide the two into a profit margin and you have handed the model a number that speaks directly to the thing it actually cares about.
2.1 Profit Margin From Revenue and Cost

Take a simple business dataset with a revenue column and a cost column. Neither one tells you, by itself, whether a given row represents a healthy business or one bleeding money. Divide the difference by revenue and you get profit_margin, a single number that answers exactly that question.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "revenue": [120000, 85000, 43000, 260000],
    "cost": [90000, 60000, 39000, 150000],
})

df["profit_margin"] = (df["revenue"] - df["cost"]) / df["revenue"]
print(df)

blocks.text: profit_margin now ranges from roughly 0.09 for the tightest margin row up to about 0.42 for the healthiest one. Neither revenue nor cost alone carried that story on its own. It only appeared once the two were combined.
2.2 Price Per Square Foot From Price and Square Footage

Real estate data gives another classic example. A price column by itself cannot tell you whether a home is a good deal, because a mansion and a small apartment can both list at the same price for completely different reasons. Divide price by square footage and you get price_per_sqft, a normalized number that lets you compare a tiny downtown condo against a sprawling suburban house on genuinely equal footing.

price_per_sqft turns out to be one of the single most predictive features in almost every real estate pricing model, often more useful than price or square_footage individually, precisely because it captures what both of those columns mean together.
2.3 Why Derived Arithmetic Features Often Win

There is a general pattern hiding behind both examples above. A raw column usually measures one thing in isolation. A well chosen ratio, difference, or product measures a relationship between things, and relationships are frequently what actually drives whatever outcome you are trying to predict. profit_margin captures the relationship between what a business earns and what it spends. price_per_sqft captures the relationship between what a home costs and how much space you get for that cost.

blocks.title: Watch for columns that only make sense combined
blocks.content: A dead giveaway that you are looking at a good arithmetic feature candidate is when two raw columns only really make sense to a human when discussed together. Nobody evaluates a company on revenue alone, or a house on price alone. If your own intuition instinctively reaches for a ratio when describing the data out loud, pandas can compute that same ratio as a column.

blocks.text: 3. Binning and Bucketing Continuous Columns
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417256-216538094.png

Sometimes the most useful version of a continuous numeric column is not the raw number at all, it is a small set of discrete categories carved out of that number's range. Turning a raw age column of 34, 61, 8, and 45 into age groups like child, teen, adult, and senior is called binning or bucketing, and pandas gives you two tools built specifically for it: pd.cut and pd.qcut.
3.1 pd.cut and Manually Chosen Boundaries

pd.cut slices a continuous column into bins using boundaries you choose yourself. You hand it a list of cutoff edges and, optionally, a label for each resulting bin, and it returns a new categorical column.

code.content:
ages = pd.DataFrame({"age": [8, 15, 34, 61, 45, 3, 70]})

ages["age_group"] = pd.cut(
    ages["age"],
    bins=[0, 12, 19, 64, 120],
    labels=["child", "teen", "adult", "senior"]
)
print(ages)

blocks.title: pd.cut bins are right inclusive by default
blocks.content: With bins=[0, 12, 19, 64, 120], a 12 year old lands in the child bucket and a 13 year old lands in teen, because each bin includes its right edge and excludes its left edge by default. Pass right=False if you want the opposite convention, and always sanity check a boundary value or two by hand the first time you write a cut call.

blocks.text: 3.2 pd.qcut and Equal Sized Quantile Bins

pd.cut requires you to already know sensible boundaries, which works well for something like age where child, teen, adult, and senior are culturally obvious cutoffs. Plenty of columns do not have obvious cutoffs like that. pd.qcut solves a different problem: instead of you choosing the boundaries, it chooses them for you so that each resulting bin contains roughly the same number of rows.

code.content:
incomes = pd.DataFrame({"income": [32000, 41000, 55000, 61000, 78000, 95000, 130000, 210000]})

incomes["income_quartile"] = pd.qcut(
    incomes["income"],
    q=4,
    labels=["low", "mid_low", "mid_high", "high"]
)
print(incomes)

blocks.text: Each of the four quartiles above ends up holding exactly two rows, since pd.qcut placed its boundaries based on where the data's own distribution splits into quarters, not on any number you supplied yourself.

blocks.title: qcut can fail on columns with lots of repeated values
blocks.content: If a column has so many duplicate values that qcut cannot find a distinct edge for every requested quantile, it raises an error by default. Pass duplicates='drop' to let it merge bins that would otherwise collide, which produces fewer than q bins but keeps the call from crashing.

blocks.text: 3.3 Why Binning Sometimes Helps a Model

It might seem like throwing away information, and in a narrow sense it is, a bucket labeled adult tells you less than the exact number 34 does. But binning can genuinely help a model when the relationship between a raw number and your target is not a straight line. Age is the classic example: risk, spending, or health outcomes rarely move in a perfectly straight line as age increases, they tend to shift in plateaus, roughly flat through most of adulthood, then stepping up sharply past some threshold. A raw linear model staring at the number 34 has to work hard to represent that kind of step shaped pattern. A model looking at the category adult versus senior gets that same step shape handed to it directly, for free.

blocks.title: Binning trades precision for shape
blocks.content: You lose the fine grained difference between a 20 year old and a 25 year old once both fall into the same adult bucket. That is a real cost. Reach for binning when you have a real reason to believe the underlying relationship is non linear or step shaped, not as a default habit applied to every numeric column you see.

blocks.text: 4. Interaction Features
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417256-556812099.png

An interaction feature captures what two columns mean together, in a way that neither column captures on its own. The general idea is that sometimes the combined effect of two variables is genuinely different from just knowing each variable in isolation, and a plain model looking at the two raw columns separately has no direct way to see that combined effect unless you hand it over as its own column.
4.1 Multiplying Two Numeric Columns
The simplest interaction feature is a straightforward multiplication of two numeric columns. Multiplying captures a magnitude that grows with both inputs at once, rather than either one alone.

A four bedroom, one bathroom house and a two bedroom, two bathroom house might average out to a similar total room count if you just summed the two columns, but they are very different homes to live in. Multiplying instead of summing lets the interaction feature reflect that a home with plenty of both bedrooms and bathrooms is meaningfully different from a home with plenty of one and almost none of the other.
4.2 Concatenating Two Categorical Columns

Interaction features are not limited to numbers. Two categorical columns can be combined the same way, by concatenating their string values into one new combined category. A clothing dataset with a size column and a color column is a good example: maybe small red items and large red items sell completely differently, a pattern that a model looking at size and color as two separate columns can struggle to pick up on its own.

blocks.title: Watch combined category cardinality before you commit to it
blocks.content: If size has 5 unique values and color has 8, size_color can have up to 40 unique combinations, and plenty of those combinations might show up in only one or two rows of your actual dataset. Run value_counts on the combined column before using it, and be ready to fall back to the two original columns if most combinations barely have any data behind them.

blocks.text: 5. Feature Creation Is a General Skill, Not Just a Pandas Trick

Zoom out for a second and notice something about the two earlier lessons in this module, Date and Time Operations and String Operations. Pulling a day of week out of a timestamp, or a review's word count out of a block of raw text, are not really separate skills from what this lesson has been building. They are the exact same feature creation mindset, applied to two specific data types. A raw timestamp on its own is often nearly useless to a model. A day of week extracted from it can be genuinely predictive. A raw block of text is nearly useless to most models too, until you derive a word count, a character count, or a keyword flag out of it.

That is really the entire point of naming feature creation as its own lesson. Whether the raw material sitting in front of you is two numeric columns, a timestamp, a block of text, or a pair of categories, the underlying question is always the same one: what new column, derived from what you already have, would actually help a model see the pattern you already know is there. Arithmetic combinations, binning, and interaction features are the general purpose tools for numeric and categorical columns. Date and time extraction and string parsing are the same tool applied to their own specific data types.
6. Domain Knowledge Is the Real Driver

blocks.alt: Domain Knowledge Is the Real Driver
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417257-889210028.png

None of the pandas mechanics in this lesson are the hard part. pd.cut, a multiplication, a string concatenation, all of that is a few minutes of syntax. The actual skill in feature creation is knowing which combination of columns is even worth trying in the first place, and that comes from understanding the problem domain you are working in, not from any automated tool.

Nobody arrives at profit_margin as a feature by randomly dividing columns against each other. They arrive at it because they understand, from real business experience, that profitability is what actually matters, and that revenue and cost only tell that story once you combine them. The same is true of price_per_sqft in real estate, of a size and color interaction in retail, of a day of week extracted from a timestamp in a churn model. Every one of those choices reflects somebody's understanding of what actually drives the outcome in that specific domain.

items: A healthcare data scientist knows which lab values interact in medically meaningful ways
A retail analyst knows which product attributes tend to interact with each other in customer behavior
A real estate specialist knows that price alone means little without square footage attached to it
None of that domain specific judgment comes packaged inside pandas itself

blocks.title: Automated feature generation tools do not replace this judgment
blocks.content: Tools exist that try to automatically generate huge numbers of candidate features by combining columns in every possible way. They can be a useful starting point for exploration, but they tend to produce an enormous pile of mostly useless columns alongside the occasional genuinely good one, and telling the difference still requires exactly the domain understanding this section is describing. Judgment is not optional here, it is the actual product.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Engineering Features for a Real Estate Dataset

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Engineering Features for a Real Estate Dataset
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417491-287429469.png

Time to put arithmetic combinations, binning, and interaction features to work together on one small, real feeling dataset. A real estate dataset arrives with price, square_footage, year_built, bedrooms, and bathrooms. None of those five raw columns individually tells the full story a pricing model needs. Three new engineered columns, built from exactly the ideas covered so far in this lesson, get it a lot closer.
7.1 The Raw Data
7.2 Creating price_per_sqft

The first engineered feature is the arithmetic combination from section 2, applied here directly. Dividing price by square footage normalizes away the size difference between these five homes, so the resulting number reflects cost efficiency instead of raw size.
7.3 Bucketing age_of_home With pd.cut

year_built is a raw year, not especially meaningful to a model on its own. Converting it into how old the home actually is, then binning that age into a small set of categories, turns it into something closer to how a buyer would actually think about a home's age.

code.content:
CURRENT_YEAR = 2026
homes["home_age_years"] = CURRENT_YEAR - homes["year_built"]

homes["age_of_home"] = pd.cut(
    homes["home_age_years"],
    bins=[-1, 5, 20, 50, 200],
    labels=["new", "recent", "established", "old"]
)
print(homes[["year_built", "home_age_years", "age_of_home"]])

blocks.title: The negative one lower boundary is a deliberate pd.cut trick
blocks.content: A brand new home built this year has an age of 0. Since pd.cut bins are right inclusive by default, a lower boundary of exactly 0 would exclude that 0 itself. Starting the first bin below zero instead guarantees a home_age_years value of 0 lands inside the new bucket rather than falling through with no bin assigned at all.

blocks.text: 7.4 Building the bedrooms_bathrooms Interaction
Bedrooms and bathrooms individually tell you something, but a home's overall livability leans heavily on how the two combine. The interaction feature from section 4 applies here without any changes.
7.5 Putting It All Together
Three brand new columns, none of which existed in the raw data, all derived using nothing more than the techniques from this lesson.

Every one of those five rows now carries information that price, square_footage, year_built, bedrooms, and bathrooms did not directly express on their own. A pricing model handed these three new columns alongside the originals has a genuinely easier job than one handed only the raw five.
8. Recap
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442417492-323933836.png

items: A feature is any individual measurable input column a model actually sees, and creating good new ones from raw data is often the single highest leverage activity in an ML project
Arithmetic combinations like profit_margin and price_per_sqft turn two raw columns into a ratio or difference that is frequently more directly predictive than either input alone
pd.cut bins a continuous column using boundaries you choose yourself, while pd.qcut computes boundaries automatically so every bin holds roughly the same number of rows
Binning can help a model see a non linear, step shaped relationship more simply than the raw continuous number would, at the cost of losing fine grained precision
Interaction features, whether multiplying two numeric columns or concatenating two categorical ones, capture a combined effect that neither column expresses by itself
Date and time extraction and string parsing from earlier in this module are the exact same feature creation mindset applied to their own specific data types
Domain knowledge, not any pandas method or automated tool, is what actually decides which new feature is worth creating in the first place
